interactions.summary: Jiang insists on keeping the Piccarda scenario inside an imaginative moral game, escalates the brother's coercion from forcing marriage to threatening their mother, and argues that this added pressure makes Piccarda's surrender intelligible.
A student predicts the brother would prevent Piccarda's suicide because his political commitment to his ally and the war effort requires keeping her alive.
A student asks why the brother cannot simply marry off another female relative instead of Piccarda.

Students keep trying to strategize alternate countermoves, but Jiang rejects those tactical escapes and keeps forcing the class toward the moral pressure point of faith, surrender, and threatened family violence.

claims.claim: Jiang treats the Piccarda episode as an imaginative exercise that should be played out like a film in order to expose the inner logic of faith, coercion, and moral choice.
He intensifies the scenario by arguing that the brother would threaten to kill their mother in order to force Piccarda out of the convent and fulfill his vow to give her as a bride.

Jiang says the brother cannot substitute another bride because the vow was specifically to give Piccarda, so the binding force of the promise depends on exact fulfillment rather than general family alliance.
He argues that once the mother is threatened, Piccarda effectively has no remaining tactical choice and therefore surrenders rather than cause both her own death and her mother's death.
A student counters that if Piccarda truly trusts God, she should believe God will protect her mother and therefore continue resisting instead of surrendering.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang explicitly asks the class to imagine they are writing a movie so the theological problem becomes dramatically visible.
signature_moments.source_phrase: let's imagine we're writing a movie
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows his preferred method: theology becomes legible only when you dramatize its choices rather than summarize doctrine.

signature_moments.moment: The brother's coercion escalates from a marriage demand to a threat to kidnap and kill the mother.
signature_moments.source_phrase: i'm going to kill her unless you come out
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the move that turns abstract free-will talk into a brutal test of what vows cost under pressure.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang treats Piccarda's surrender as the point where individual martyrdom collides with responsibility for another life.
signature_moments.source_phrase: to end up killing yourself and your mother
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sharpens the class's core Dante question: when does fidelity to God stop being solitary heroism and become entanglement with other people's fates?

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's way of forcing the class to inhabit Piccarda's situation imaginatively rather than discuss it as static doctrine.
The act Jiang assigns to Piccarda once the threat expands to include her mother, making surrender a test of faith, coercion, and responsibility rather than simple weakness.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-06-18 Jiang pushes the Piccarda problem away from textual exegesis and into an increasingly cinematic coercion scenario so the class can test what faith would demand under escalating threats.

uncertainty_notes.note: ASR likely mangles 'convent' as 'comment' while Jiang describes the brother threatening Piccarda after entering the convent.
